Nigeria’s Development Cooperation Dashboard Profiled at the OECD Development Finance Data Forum

The Nigeria Development Cooperation Dashboard was profiled in a keynote address by H.E. Dr. Doris Uzoka-Anite, Minister of State for Budget and Economic Planning, Federal Republic of Nigeria, at the OECD Development Finance Data Forum in Paris.

Recognition of the Dashboard as a practical instrument for managing development cooperation

The Dashboard is designed to integrate closely with countries’ own public financial management processes, rather than simply being an additional piece of software that countries have to maintain, manage and provide data to. H.E. Dr. Doris Uzoka-Anite said:

“The Nigeria Development Cooperation Dashboard is evolving beyond a conventional database. It is becoming a practical instrument for planning, coordination, transparency and accountability in development cooperation.”
Interoperability with international standards, including IATI

As the first system in the world to import IATI data on an ongoing basis, the Dashboard ensures that capturing data on a wide range of development partners’ activities is sustainable. It keeps the burden of data collection low while capturing high-quality, granular and timely data from partners:

“The Dashboard consolidates information on development cooperation activities and resources reported by development partners, principally through the International Aid Transparency Initiative. It enables Government to see who is providing resources, what is being financed, where resources are being deployed, the scale of financing involved, and the development objectives being supported.”

Over the last year, we have further enhanced the interoperability of the Dashboard by strengthening the IFMIS integration, providing for automatic syncing of results data captured in DHIS2, and developing more complete API documentation.

We are continuously improving and developing the Dashboard. Going forward, we will make it possible to capture even more granular data in the Dashboard, and further streamline integrations with other systems. At the core of our design principles, we always strive to provide additional functionality while avoiding additional complexity, and constantly seek ways to simplify the existing system.
Improving development outcomes in Liberia: the Liberia Development Dashboard
The Liberia Development Dashboard has been used by a wide range of development actors. This blog describes the Dashboard’s contribution to improving development outcomes in Liberia.

At the same time, budgetary pressures and political changes in donor countries are leading to a reduction in support for official development assistance (ODA). In this context, it has become more important than ever to ensure that available funding is being used well.

Since 2019, funded by Sweden, ODI Global has been working with the Liberian Ministry of Finance and Development Planning to build a system to track development funding and activities: the Liberia Development Dashboard. The Dashboard, developed by ODI Global and Emergentally, was made public in 2020, and tracking began in June 2023. Since then, it has been visited over 38,000 times (and almost 20,000 times in the last 12 months). The Dashboard includes user-friendly but powerful visual graphics, with summaries of planned and actual spending by funder, sector, sustainable development goals (SDGs) and location (e.g. counties). It also includes summary and detailed information on results achieved by specific projects, and progress against the National Development Plan,
the ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development
. Data is of increasingly high quality and easy to enter and keep up to date. All the data is publicly available and can be downloaded in various formats.
Other systems – often called AIMS, or Aid Information Management Systems – provide similar functionality, but
their track record is not very strong
; they can be hard to maintain, leading to poor-quality data and limited use. This is why, when delivering the Dashboard, we paid particular attention to simplicity and usability.

We made data collection forms simpler and more user-friendly, while allowing data to be uploaded from Excel and imported from IATI, the International Aid Transparency Initiative. Liberia is the first country in the world to import IATI data, significantly reducing the burden of data collection while improving the quality of data collected. We also worked to ensure the data was useful and usable by a wide range of stakeholders.

Liberia provided concrete use examples at last year’s IATI Members’ Assembly in Bogotá, Colombia. When the President wanted information on energy projects, it took less than half an hour to extract the data required to make a decision on new loans, considering implementation progress to date. This used both detailed financial and results data. In another case, location mapping data in the Dashboard was used in an analysis of food security by identifying feeder road projects that made more remote parts of the country accessible.

We know informally that development partners have used the system to coordinate among themselves; in one case, two development partners realised that they were working in the same subsector in the same counties. Development partners have used the Dashboard when designing new projects and programmes, as the data gives them a ready overview of existing activities.

Sustainability of the Dashboard has been a key concern. The most important aspect of this is strengthening the value proposition: ensuring the system is useful to a range of stakeholders, while minimising the burden of keeping it going. Long-term, flexible grant support from the Swedish Embassy gave us the time and resources to develop a strong system with a clear value proposition. Day-to-day management of the system and all data entry is undertaken by MFDP, and the Dashboard is now hosted on Liberian government servers. Funding ongoing development and adding new features, to maintain the relevance of the system in an evolving policy context, is also to some extent about the value proposition: stakeholders will invest in a system if it is delivering value. But it is also about minimising the cost, which we are doing through offering the system in other countries and contexts. While each context is different, many needs are shared, enabling economies of scale.

The upgraded Liberia Development Dashboard was launched in November 2025, including additional features on NGO registration, accreditation and reporting. The intention is to both streamling processes and increase the focus on development outcomes, in an era of increasingly scarce resources.
The Dashboard has proved useful to a broad array of actors, in government, among development partners, and throughout media and NGOs. This is a model that could be adopted by other countries.
